Title: Perceived Organizational Support in the Face of Algorithmic Management: A Conceptual Model
Snippet: The use of algorithmic management is also expected to disrupt the POS antecedents of supervisor support and procedural fairness. Insofar as algorithmic management systems necessitate the minimization of human intervention to benefit from algorithmic-efficiencies, algorithmic management marks a radical departure from earlier managerial logic, which relied heavily on human supervisors to direct work [5,6,15]. In algorithmically managed contexts, most managerial and decisionmaking processes are reduced into a set of opaque algorithmic processes that are both complex and inaccessible to the typical worker [1,6,8]. Thus, given the scarcity of human intervention and considering that workers' subjective interpretations of procedural justice play a key role in forming perceptions of organizational support, both antecedents of supervisor support and procedural justice will be disrupted by algorithmic management [8]. As such, a new theory of POS is required for algorithmically-managed gig-work.

Title: Fair Sharing for Sharing Economy Platforms
Snippet: In this work, we focus on goal (a), investigating the trade-off between utility for customers and fairness to providers, and leaving other scenarios as subjects of future work. 

In a marked departure from past efforts on defining fairness in search and recommendation systems [17,19], we add a temporal dimension to the notion of fairness. We argue that a fair matching platform would be something that distributes the exposure of providers to customers over time in a fair way. The exact fairness notions are discussed in Section 2. 

The advantage of introducing the time dimension into the notion of fairness in sharing economy platforms is two fold: (i) The fairness notion becomes more relaxed than the constrained requirement of being fair with respect to every matching, and (ii) Abstractly, the problem maps to one of fair division of a constrained resource (in this context, the exposure of providers to customers) over time. There is a long line of work on bringing fairness in generalized processor sharing algorithms [2,29], which could be applied in a temporally fair matching system. 

In summary, in this position paper, we make two contributions: (i) we provide a systematic way to think about fairness in sharing economy platforms, and (ii) by introducing the temporal dimension to the notion of fairness in such platforms, we enable reuse of the existing techniques for fairness in processor scheduling. In future work, we would go beyond fairness for providers, and consider fairness for all members of the sharing ecosystem. Subsequently, we would like to investigate RQ2 and RQ3 as outlined earlier, to provide a comprehensive understanding and potentially required addition of fairness in today's sharing economy platforms.

Title: Resource Scheduling in Edge Computing: Architecture, Taxonomy, Open Issues and Future Research Directions
Snippet: Fairness and load balancing can be mentioned among the scheduling objectives that have received less attention in previous articles, particularly in survey papers. This section briefly reviews these two factors and the related scheduling methods. The concept of fairness has been explored from several social justice and welfare economics perspectives, including those advanced by Nash Jr [128] and Rawls [129]. As per Rawls's theory of justice, resources should be allocated to the least fortunate users to increase satisfaction and utility to the greatest extent possible. The Nash bargaining theory offers an alternative view, which states that resources should be reallocated to those who will benefit more from them than those who lose them. 

Schedulers must be fair as one of their essential characteristics. Schedulers were traditionally designed to share resources between processes fairly, which had been interpreted in the context of tasks. Schedulers must treat users fairly rather than just tasks, as recently realized [130]. Through a fair scheduling system, competing users get their fair share of resources over a long period of time. When dealing with connection and disconnection from Roadside Units (RSUs) as the vehicle moves from one RSU to another, Strugeon et al. [131] proposed an agent-based approach to ensure long-term fair allocation of computing resources in the autonomous driving domain. In order to assess whether resource allocation is fair, a fairness ratio is employed. Zhao et al. [132] formulated the UAV's energy consumption minimization problem as a mixed integer nonlinear programming problem, where the UAV's trajectory, resource allocation, task decision, and bits scheduling are jointly considered to ensure fairness among Ground Nodes (GN). In addition to protecting the UAV from being overwhelmed by the data from one or more GNs, this approach guarantees fairness across all operations, such as local computing, task offloading for computing and caching, and avoids the situation where the UAV caches all offloaded bits. Xu et al. [133] developed a job scheduling algorithm based on Berger's distributive justice theory in cloud environment. A fair scheduling model with trust enhancement for the cloudfog-edge environments was described in [134]. Blockchain technology is used to build a decentralized trust framework to address the service credibility.

Title: Algorithmic surveillance and workers’ compliance: The role of trust, privacy concerns, and fairness in online crowdwork
Snippet: Traditional discussions of organizational justice (for an overview, see Greenberg, 1987) have long recognized the importance of fairness in both organizational procedures and outcome distributions (e.g., Procedural Justice Theory: Thibaut and Walker, 1975;Equity Theory: Adams, 1965). While a detailed review of organizational justice theories is beyond the scope of this study, we argue that fairness judgments are central to understanding workers' responses to algorithmic surveillance systems (Alder and Ambrose, 2005;Alge, 2001;Stanton, 2000). 

Fairness is often considered a global perception of appropriateness, shaped by procedural and distributive justice (Colquitt and Zipay, 2015). Procedural fairness, in particular, focuses on the perceived legitimacy and transparency of organizational processes rather than just the outcomes they produce (Leventhal, 1980;Thibaut and Walker, 1975). In algorithmic management, procedural fairness is particularly salient, as surveillance and decision-making processes occur through automated systems that can obscure the rationale behind workplace decisions (Newman et al., 2020;Starke et al., 2022). The inability of workers to challenge or appeal algorithmic assessments has been identified as key concerns that undermine procedural fairness perceptions (Jabagi et al., 2024). 

Arguably, the algorithmic management systems these platforms deploy highlight the power imbalance and information asymmetries in the triadic relationship between the platform, requesters, and the workers, thereby impeding fairness assessments (Duggan et al., 2020;Shanahan and Smith, 2023). The platform organization is the only party in this relationship with full access to and control over the data, processes, and rules of the platform (Jabagi et al., 2019). Indeed, perceived unfairness related to online crowdwork, and their algorithmic governance styles has been repeatedly documented (e.g., Jabagi et al., 2024). Shanahan and Smith (2023) found that workers subjected to algorithmic surveillance sought ways to maintain fair exchanges between workers and the platform by flouting the rules by pooling their experiences and sharing tricks that could help circumvent platform surveillance.

Title: Predation, acceleration, and loss of control: a multilevel theoretical framework for algorithmic time politics and the occupational health of platform workers
Snippet: " Algorithmic time politics refers to the asymmetric power relation established between workers and platforms through the systematic manipulation of temporal rhythm, temporal allocation, and temporal ownership by algorithms in platform labor, which in turn produces identifiable and predictable damaging effects across the three dimensions of physiological health, mental health, and occupational safety. The concept encompasses three interlocking operational dimensions: 

The temporal ownership dimension addresses the question "who decides how workers' time is used?" In traditional employment relations, workers transfer the right to use their labor time within a contractually specified scope, and the boundaries of this ownership are at least nominally protected by legal contracts. Under the conditions of ambiguous employment relations in the platform economy, however, workers have in practice partially lost the capacity to claim ownership over their time. Through compulsory task-assignment mechanisms, overtime penalty mechanisms, and fragmented waiting mechanisms, algorithms de facto appropriate workers' temporal ownership. It is worth emphasizing that "ownership" here is not a concept in the legal sense, but rather refers to workers' substantive capacity to autonomously control whether and how their own time is utilized. Even if workers are legally designated as "independent contractors, " the reality remains that they cannot autonomously determine the manner in which their time is used; in effect, the substance of ownership has already been hollowed out. 

The temporal rhythm dimension addresses the question "at what speed and tempo is labor performed?" The dynamic scheduling of algorithms renders temporal rhythms non-standardized, instantaneous, and unpredictable. Mbare et al., in a study of Finnish food delivery couriers, found that algorithmic management increases work demands, reduces work control, and restricts workplace support, and that the combination of these factors produces negative psychosocial effects both directly and indirectly (15). This unpredictability of rhythm means that workers cannot plan their energy allocation in the way that traditional employees can-they do not know whether the next minute will be busy or idle, or whether they can finish work at a predictable time today. They are thus constantly maintained in a state of alertness and stress. 

The temporal allocation dimension addresses the question "where does the boundary between labor time and life time lie?"

In this work, we focus on goal (a), investigating the trade-off between utility for customers and fairness to providers, and leaving other scenarios as subjects of future work. 

In a marked departure from past efforts on defining fairness in search and recommendation systems [17,19], we add a temporal dimension to the notion of fairness. We argue that a fair matching platform would be something that distributes the exposure of providers to customers over time in a fair way. The exact fairness notions are discussed in Section 2. 

The advantage of introducing the time dimension into the notion of fairness in sharing economy platforms is two fold: (i) The fairness notion becomes more relaxed than the constrained requirement of being fair with respect to every matching, and (ii) Abstractly, the problem maps to one of fair division of a constrained resource (in this context, the exposure of providers to customers) over time. As per Rawls's theory of justice, resources should be allocated to the least fortunate users to increase satisfaction and utility to the greatest extent possible. The Nash bargaining theory offers an alternative view, which states that resources should be reallocated to those who will benefit more from them than those who lose them. 

Schedulers must be fair as one of their essential characteristics. Schedulers were traditionally designed to share resources between processes fairly, which had been interpreted in the context of tasks. Schedulers must treat users fairly rather than just tasks, as recently realized [130]. Through a fair scheduling system, competing users get their fair share of resources over a long period of time. When dealing with connection and disconnection from Roadside Units (RSUs) as the vehicle moves from one RSU to another, Strugeon et al. [131] proposed an agent-based approach to ensure long-term fair allocation of computing resources in the autonomous driving domain. In order to assess whether resource allocation is fair, a fairness ratio is employed. Zhao et al. [132] formulated the UAV's energy consumption minimization problem as a mixed integer nonlinear programming problem, where the UAV's trajectory, resource allocation, task decision, and bits scheduling are jointly considered to ensure fairness among Ground Nodes (GN). Traditional discussions of organizational justice (for an overview, see Greenberg, 1987) have long recognized the importance of fairness in both organizational procedures and outcome distributions (e.g., Procedural Justice Theory: Thibaut and Walker, 1975;Equity Theory: Adams, 1965). While a detailed review of organizational justice theories is beyond the scope of this study, we argue that fairness judgments are central to understanding workers' responses to algorithmic surveillance systems (Alder and Ambrose, 2005;Alge, 2001;Stanton, 2000). 

Fairness is often considered a global perception of appropriateness, shaped by procedural and distributive justice (Colquitt and Zipay, 2015). Procedural fairness, in particular, focuses on the perceived legitimacy and transparency of organizational processes rather than just the outcomes they produce (Leventhal, 1980;Thibaut and Walker, 1975). In algorithmic management, procedural fairness is particularly salient, as surveillance and decision-making processes occur through automated systems that can obscure the rationale behind workplace decisions (Newman et al., 2020;Starke et al., 2022). The inability of workers to challenge or appeal algorithmic assessments has been identified as key concerns that undermine procedural fairness perceptions (Jabagi et al., 2024). 

Arguably, the algorithmic management systems these platforms deploy highlight the power imbalance and information asymmetries in the triadic relationship between the platform, requesters, and the workers, thereby impeding fairness assessments (Duggan et al., 2020;Shanahan and Smith, 2023). The platform organization is the only party in this relationship with full access to and control over the data, processes, and rules of the platform (Jabagi et al., 2019). Indeed, perceived unfairness related to online crowdwork, and their algorithmic governance styles has been repeatedly documented (e.g., Jabagi et al., 2024). Shanahan and Smith (2023) found that workers subjected to algorithmic surveillance sought ways to maintain fair exchanges between workers and the platform by flouting the rules by pooling their experiences and sharing tricks that could help circumvent platform surveillance.

" Algorithmic time politics refers to the asymmetric power relation established between workers and platforms through the systematic manipulation of temporal rhythm, temporal allocation, and temporal ownership by algorithms in platform labor, which in turn produces identifiable and predictable damaging effects across the three dimensions of physiological health, mental health, and occupational safety. The concept encompasses three interlocking operational dimensions: 

The temporal ownership dimension addresses the question "who decides how workers' time is used?" In traditional employment relations, workers transfer the right to use their labor time within a contractually specified scope, and the boundaries of this ownership are at least nominally protected by legal contracts. Under the conditions of ambiguous employment relations in the platform economy, however, workers have in practice partially lost the capacity to claim ownership over their time. Through compulsory task-assignment mechanisms, overtime penalty mechanisms, and fragmented waiting mechanisms, algorithms de facto appropriate workers' temporal ownership. It is worth emphasizing that "ownership" here is not a concept in the legal sense, but rather refers to workers' substantive capacity to autonomously control whether and how their own time is utilized. Even if workers are legally designated as "independent contractors, " the reality remains that they cannot autonomously determine the manner in which their time is used; in effect, the substance of ownership has already been hollowed out. 

The temporal rhythm dimension addresses the question "at what speed and tempo is labor performed?" The dynamic scheduling of algorithms renders temporal rhythms non-standardized, instantaneous, and unpredictable. Mbare et al., in a study of Finnish food delivery couriers, found that algorithmic management increases work demands, reduces work control, and restricts workplace support, and that the combination of these factors produces negative psychosocial effects both directly and indirectly (15). This unpredictability of rhythm means that workers cannot plan their energy allocation in the way that traditional employees can-they do not know whether the next minute will be busy or idle, or whether they can finish work at a predictable time today. They are thus constantly maintained in a state of alertness and stress. 

The temporal allocation dimension addresses the question "where does the boundary between labor time and life time lie?"

Title: Matching Policy Design for Gig Platforms with "Priority" Features
Snippet: In recent years, gig platforms like Uber and DoorDash have implemented strategies to boost gig drivers' earnings during peak hours. Uber's 'back-to-back' feature allows drivers to accept new trips while still on route, and Uber Eats' 'Batch Order Route' initiative allows drivers to pick up multiple deliveries from different locations, which may result in multiple tops before one order is delivered. Despite revenue gains, these features lead to user complaints about extended waiting times. In response, platforms introduce features like Uber Eats' 'Priority Delivery' and Uber's 'Priority', where customers pay an extra subscription fee for guaranteed reduced waiting times.
This paper focuses on designing matching policies to enhance system revenue while limiting customer waiting times. We present a hybrid model combining online matching and queue theory for quantitative analysis of users' waiting times. Additionally, we introduce an LP-based sampling framework and a unified queue-theory-based method for evaluating online performance. Comprehensive experiments on real datasets validate our theoretical findings, highlighting the efficiency of our matching framework in promoting profit and meeting committed waiting times.

Title: Machine Learning Based Prediction of Uber Ride Demand and Fare Pricing
Snippet: Uber and other ride-hailing systems operate in spatiotemporal dynamics; having accurate ride demand prediction and fare pricing greatly influences customers’ experience as well as system efficiency. According to current research that splits Uber’s operations into demand forecasting and fare pricing, both tasks are affected by highly similar external factors that include time attributes, pickup and drop-off locations, distances between two points, weather, etc. This paper models both ride demand forecasting and fare price prediction with a Gradient Boosting Regressor (GBR)-based machine learning framework. Title: AI AS AN APPROACH TO ANALYZING UBER'S BUSINESS ENVIRONMENT IN THE TRANSPORTATION SERVICES SECTOR
Snippet: Founded in 2009, Uber is a multinational company headquartered in San Francisco (Vultur & Enel, 2020, p. 16), Uber provides a digital platform supported by a vast network of transportation services, primarily acting as an intermediary between taxi drivers and customers (passengers). In addition to ride-hailing, Uber offers food delivery services, freight services, and new transportation options such as electric bicycles, along with electronic support platforms (UBER, 2019, pp. 3-5). Drivers pay Uber a commission based on their revenue (Angrist, Caldwell, & Jonathan, 2021, p. 272), which ranges from 20% to 30% (Vultur & Enel, 2020, p. 16). The company has entered numerous international markets, operating in 72 countries, with key services offered in the United States, Canada, Latin America, Europe, Asia, the Middle East, and select African nations (UBER, 2022, p. 4) The GPS system has become a standard tool for Uber's team, especially as traffic congestion and peak hours have led to losses for e-taxi drivers and customer dissatisfaction. These issues arose from limitations in Uber's ridesharing platform (Sawhney, Shah, Yu, & Rubtsov, 2019, p. 1). In response, Uber's team developed a more accurate platform utilizing artificial intelligence, which enhances the ability to track taxi locations and facilitate customer pickup. This system also identifies critical routes to optimize arrival times while considering traffic conditions (UBER, 2019). 

The figure 1 illustrates the processes of routing and pricing for Uber's taxi services through a hybrid model for estimating time of arrival (ETA) and subsequent pricing. This model is termed "hybrid" as it combines digital operations reliant on artificial intelligence with a set of algorithms that determine critical routing and pricing based on demand-influencing factors (such as traffic conditions, weather, time of day, peak hours, etc.). The process involves the following stages: 

• Model Inputs: The inputs for the hybrid model consist of receiving requests and determining customer locations on the map. Subsequently, traffic conditions are assessed using intelligent recognition technology and marked on the map. In another phase, the locations of the nearest available drivers are identified for task assignment.

Title: Dynamic Trip-Vehicle Dispatch with Scheduled and On-Demand Requests
Snippet: The growth in location-tracking technology, the popularity of smartphones, and the reduced cost in mobile network communications have led to a revolution in mobility and the prevalent use of on-demand transportation systems, with a tremendous positive societal impact on personal mobility, pollution, and congestion. Recently, more and more transportation service providers start to support both on-demand ride requests posted in real time and rides scheduled in advance, providing riders with more flexible and reliable service. For example, ridehailing platforms such as Uber match drivers or vehicles (we will use drivers and vehicles interchangeably) and riders in real time upon riders' request and also allow the riders to schedule rides in advance. Companies like Curb, Shenzhou Zhuanche and ComfortDelGro and Supershuttle transform traditional taxi-hailing, chauffeured car service, and shuttle service to satisfy both types of requests [Apple Inc., 2018;ComfortDelGro Inc., 2018]. 

The presence of both scheduled requests and on-demand requests leads to new challenges in the task of tripvehicle dispatch to service providers. Accepting scheduled requests is a double-edged sword: on one hand, such requests reduce the demand uncertainty and give the service provider more time to prepare and optimize these trips; On the other hand, certain scheduled requests may lead to waste in time on the way to serve them or prevent the assigned vehicle from serving more valuable ondemand requests. Some systems such as Uber simply treat scheduled requests as regular on-demand requests when their pick-up time is due and directly apply an existing dispatch algorithm for on-demand requests. Such practice, however, overlooks a fundamental difference between scheduled and on-demand requests: the rider expect to be picked up on time for sure once their scheduled request is accepted, i.e., it is a commitment that the platform must fulfill. Many scheduled requests are for important purposes, such as going to the airport to catch a flight or attending an important meeting. Failing to serve these rides could hurt the credibility of the service provider and its long-term sustainability. To the best of our knowledge, no existing work can deal with these essential challenges. 

In this paper, we fill the gap and provide the first study on trip-vehicle dispatch with both scheduled and on-demand requests. We consider a two-stage decision-making process.

snippet.text:
The growth in location-tracking technology, the popularity of smartphones, and the reduced cost in mobile network communications have led to a revolution in mobility and the prevalent use of on-demand transportation systems, with a tremendous positive societal impact on personal mobility, pollution, and congestion. Recently, more and more transportation service providers start to support both on-demand ride requests posted in real time and rides scheduled in advance, providing riders with more flexible and reliable service. For example, ridehailing platforms such as Uber match drivers or vehicles (we will use drivers and vehicles interchangeably) and riders in real time upon riders' request and also allow the riders to schedule rides in advance. Companies like Curb, Shenzhou Zhuanche and ComfortDelGro and Supershuttle transform traditional taxi-hailing, chauffeured car service, and shuttle service to satisfy both types of requests [Apple Inc., 2018;ComfortDelGro Inc., 2018]. 

The presence of both scheduled requests and on-demand requests leads to new challenges in the task of tripvehicle dispatch to service providers. Accepting scheduled requests is a double-edged sword: on one hand, such requests reduce the demand uncertainty and give the service provider more time to prepare and optimize these trips; On the other hand, certain scheduled requests may lead to waste in time on the way to serve them or prevent the assigned vehicle from serving more valuable ondemand requests. Some systems such as Uber simply treat scheduled requests as regular on-demand requests when their pick-up time is due and directly apply an existing dispatch algorithm for on-demand requests. Such practice, however, overlooks a fundamental difference between scheduled and on-demand requests: the rider expect to be picked up on time for sure once their scheduled request is accepted, i.e., it is a commitment that the platform must fulfill. Many scheduled requests are for important purposes, such as going to the airport to catch a flight or attending an important meeting. Failing to serve these rides could hurt the credibility of the service provider and its long-term sustainability. To the best of our knowledge, no existing work can deal with these essential challenges. 

In this paper, we fill the gap and provide the first study on trip-vehicle dispatch with both scheduled and on-demand requests. We consider a two-stage decision-making process.

documents.title: Matching Policy Design for Gig Platforms with "Priority" Features
documents.snippet:
In recent years, gig platforms like Uber and DoorDash have implemented strategies to boost gig drivers' earnings during peak hours. Uber's 'back-to-back' feature allows drivers to accept new trips while still on route, and Uber Eats' 'Batch Order Route' initiative allows drivers to pick up multiple deliveries from different locations, which may result in multiple tops before one order is delivered. Despite revenue gains, these features lead to user complaints about extended waiting times. In response, platforms introduce features like Uber Eats' 'Priority Delivery' and Uber's 'Priority', where customers pay an extra subscription fee for guaranteed reduced waiting times.
This paper focuses on designing matching policies to enhance system revenue while limiting customer waiting times. We present a hybrid model combining online matching and queue theory for quantitative analysis of users' waiting times. Additionally, we introduce an LP-based sampling framework and a unified queue-theory-based method for evaluating online performance. Comprehensive experiments on real datasets validate our theoretical findings, highlighting the efficiency of our matching framework in promoting profit and meeting committed waiting times.

documents.title: Machine Learning Based Prediction of Uber Ride Demand and Fare Pricing
documents.snippet: Uber and other ride-hailing systems operate in spatiotemporal dynamics; having accurate ride demand prediction and fare pricing greatly influences customers’ experience as well as system efficiency. According to current research that splits Uber’s operations into demand forecasting and fare pricing, both tasks are affected by highly similar external factors that include time attributes, pickup and drop-off locations, distances between two points, weather, etc. This paper models both ride demand forecasting and fare price prediction with a Gradient Boosting Regressor (GBR)-based machine learning framework. Our proposed model takes multidimensional spatiotemporal features as input to capture nonlinearities between demand surge and dynamic prices. Our results surpass previous approaches on all tasks regarding efficiency and accuracy. Furthermore, we demonstrate that dynamic pricing can help the optimization of this objective so Uber can make better dispatching decisions of drivers and improve decision-making using intelligent ride-hailing considering demand and price together

documents.snippet:
Founded in 2009, Uber is a multinational company headquartered in San Francisco (Vultur & Enel, 2020, p. 16), Uber provides a digital platform supported by a vast network of transportation services, primarily acting as an intermediary between taxi drivers and customers (passengers). In addition to ride-hailing, Uber offers food delivery services, freight services, and new transportation options such as electric bicycles, along with electronic support platforms (UBER, 2019, pp. 3-5). Drivers pay Uber a commission based on their revenue (Angrist, Caldwell, & Jonathan, 2021, p. 272), which ranges from 20% to 30% (Vultur & Enel, 2020, p. 16). The company has entered numerous international markets, operating in 72 countries, with key services offered in the United States, Canada, Latin America, Europe, Asia, the Middle East, and select African nations (UBER, 2022, p. 4) The GPS system has become a standard tool for Uber's team, especially as traffic congestion and peak hours have led to losses for e-taxi drivers and customer dissatisfaction. These issues arose from limitations in Uber's ridesharing platform (Sawhney, Shah, Yu, & Rubtsov, 2019, p. 1). In response, Uber's team developed a more accurate platform utilizing artificial intelligence, which enhances the ability to track taxi locations and facilitate customer pickup. This system also identifies critical routes to optimize arrival times while considering traffic conditions (UBER, 2019). 

The figure 1 illustrates the processes of routing and pricing for Uber's taxi services through a hybrid model for estimating time of arrival (ETA) and subsequent pricing. This model is termed "hybrid" as it combines digital operations reliant on artificial intelligence with a set of algorithms that determine critical routing and pricing based on demand-influencing factors (such as traffic conditions, weather, time of day, peak hours, etc.). The process involves the following stages: 

• Model Inputs: The inputs for the hybrid model consist of receiving requests and determining customer locations on the map. Subsequently, traffic conditions are assessed using intelligent recognition technology and marked on the map. In another phase, the locations of the nearest available drivers are identified for task assignment.

Below is a synthesis of the main findings on temporality justice under algorithmic management—how algorithmic systems configure work and time, how that produces temporal injustices, how workers experience and resist them, and what remedies and design principles are emerging across management, HCI, sociology, and legal/HR perspectives.

Defining temporality justice in algorithmic management
- Algorithmic management shifts core managerial functions—monitoring, scheduling, goal-setting, performance management, compensation, and termination—into automated systems that operate on real-time data and predictive analytics, often reducing or removing human discretion in the loop <cite id="f68a709a-2">In contrast, algorithmic management entrusts managerial functions such as monitoring, performance assessment, scheduling, goal‑setting, compensation, and even dismissal to algorithms and automated systems</cite> <cite id="f68a709a-2">Enabled by real‑time data collection, predictive analytics, and digital platforms, algorithmic management enables organizations to manage dispersed labor at scale with unprecedented precision</cite> <cite id="ec3d7b1f-3">AM refers to the use of increasingly intelligent algorithms to automate and optimize coordination and control; Parent‑Rocheleau and Parker identified six main functions: monitoring, goal setting, performance management, scheduling, compensation, and job termination</cite>. 
- Justice concerns arise because algorithmic neutrality is an illusion: optimization embodies normative assumptions about performance, risk, and merit, and can reproduce distributive and procedural injustices absent discriminatory intent <cite id="f68a709a-0">Empirical research demonstrates that algorithmic systems can perpetuate distributive and procedural injustices by reproducing historical inequalities or prioritizing efficiency over fairness; justice must be explicitly articulated and safeguarded within managerial decision frameworks</cite>. 
- Temporality justice focuses on whether algorithmic systems fairly govern rhythms, pacing, waiting, and the boundaries between work time and personal time; it asks whether control over time is distributed fairly and whether workers can plan, consent to, and contest temporal demands <cite id="ec3d7b1f-2">Algorithms act as machines that make time logically controllable and produce measurable time effects and rhythms; real‑time effects unfold as specific temporal conditions composed by different patterns of pace with socio‑technical arrangements</cite> <cite id="ec3d7b1f-4">Algorithmic time politics refers to asymmetric power relations established through systematic manipulation of temporal rhythm, allocation, and ownership, producing damaging effects across physiological, mental, and occupational safety dimensions</cite>.

Mechanisms that shape temporal control and justice
- Real-time quantification and surveillance. Platforms and systems track location, routes, working time, and every step, turning performance into streams of quantified data that are compared to baselines and projected into predictions to direct and evaluate work <cite id="ec3d7b1f-1">Digital systems meticulously organize, monitor, and measure work; performance data, working hours, and shifts are stored and visualized; tracking mechanisms are crucial for workforce management and create knowledge-asymmetry power imbalances favoring the platform</cite> <cite id="ec3d7b1f-3">Algorithms assign tasks, communicate with workers, and evaluate performance; algorithmic matching and controlling are core mechanisms</cite>. 
- Opacity and triangular visibility. Automated systems create information asymmetries—employers and often algorithm designers hold more knowledge than workers—undermining procedural justice and perceived organizational support that depends on accessible, fair processes <cite id="f68a709a-2">Algorithmic systems create triangular visibility regimes with information asymmetries where employers and algorithm designers hold more knowledge than workers</cite> <cite id="f68a709a-3">As algorithmic efficiencies minimize human intervention, workers’ interpretations of procedural justice are disrupted, implying a new theory of perceived organizational support for gig work</cite>. 
- Ranking, penalties, and volatility. Control is enforced through numeric rankings, fines, and dynamic dispatching that can shift workload intensity and timing unpredictably, shaping workers’ expectations and agency over time <cite id="ec3d7b1f-3">AM integrates algorithmic matching and controlling; ranking systems, fines, and incentives are used for performance governance</cite> <cite id="ec3d7b1f-4">Compulsory task-assignment and overtime penalty mechanisms appropriate workers’ temporal ownership; dynamic scheduling renders rhythms non‑standardized and instantaneous</cite>. 

Main findings on temporality justice

Temporal ownership: control over work-life boundaries and consent
- Algorithmic systems increasingly appropriate workers’ temporal ownership—the substantive capacity to decide how and when their time is used—even when legal contracts classify them as independent, by compulsory assignment, opaque ranking, and fragmented waiting, leaving workers with hollow autonomy over their schedules <cite id="ec3d7b1f-4">Algorithms de facto appropriate workers’ temporal ownership via compulsory task-assignment, overtime penalty mechanisms, and fragmented waiting; “ownership” here refers to substantive control over how time is used, which is hollowed out despite independent contractor status</cite>. 
- This erosion of temporal ownership is experienced as intensified control: workers face real-time tracking and automated penalties for deviations, reducing the predictability of when work begins and ends and compressing personal and work time <cite id="ec3d7b1f-1">Tracking mechanisms store and visualize performance data and shifts; algorithmic monitoring and real-time tracking create knowledge-asymmetry power imbalances</cite> <cite id="f68a709a-2">The shift from human oversight to software-mediated governance introduces asymmetries and reenacts power asymmetries with new challenges for worker autonomy and organizational justice</cite>. 
- Resistance emerges through work “games”—patterns of consented or non-consented tactics to negotiate the system’s rules—showing that while platforms automate control, workers simultaneously exercise agency to reclaim small temporal leeway within constrained spaces <cite id="e793ee69-4">In an Amazon fulfillment center, labor-tracking systems render labor as numbers and workers deploy active/passive consenting-resistance and non-consenting resistance; analyzing concurrent consent and resistance clarifies reactions to algorithms</cite> <cite id="e793ee69-0">HCI work emphasizes that workers’ reactivity to quantified metrics can become new regimes of control; understanding everyday impacts and counteractions is necessary to design regulatory interventions</cite>.

Temporal rhythm: speed, unpredictability, and psychosocial harm
- Dynamic scheduling and predictive control instantaneously shift task availability, producing non-standardized, unpredictable rhythms that undermine workers’ ability to allocate energy and plan, increasing alertness and stress and degrading psychosocial conditions <cite id="ec3d7b1f-4">Dynamic scheduling renders temporal rhythms non-standardized, instantaneous, and unpredictable; unpredictability prevents workers from planning energy allocation, maintaining a state of alertness and stress</cite>. 
- Empirical studies in platform delivery show algorithmic management increases demands and reduces control, with combined effects on mental and physical health; unpredictability of rhythm is a core driver of strain <cite id="ec3d7b1f-4">Mbare et al. found algorithmic management increases work demands, reduces work control, and restricts support, producing negative psychosocial effects; unpredictability of rhythm means workers cannot plan busy/idle periods or finish times</cite>. 
- Across industries, the integration of passive “stochastic machine witnesses” and active monitoring shifts accountability to workers, compressing rhythm into continuous measurable streams that normalize speed and punish latency <cite id="e793ee69-2">Contemporary monitoring is mediated by stochastic machine witnesses; systems require workers to document tasks and shift accountability onto them, extending control across channels</cite>. 
- HCI and STS theories emphasize that algorithms do not just measure time; they “make time” and generate new rhythms and cadences, shaping what counts as punctual, productive, and deviant, and producing temporal inequalities that are not self-evident to workers <cite id="ec3d7b1f-2">Algorithms inherit and impart orders as a continuous string of interpenetrating prior and subsequent actions; they are algorhythms that make time controllable and produce measurable time effects and rhythms; real-time does not mean a flat “now,” but specific patterns of pace</cite>.

Temporal allocation: fairness in scheduling, waiting, and penalties
- Fairness is entangled with optimization trade-offs: penalties for idleness or lateness, and weights for job completion times, can systematically disadvantage some workers depending on how costs are modeled, revealing the normative embedding of “fairness” in objective functions <cite id="28b71dfc-1">Dynamic idle time penalty mechanisms adapt penalty weights over iterations to balance exploration and exploitation, treating longer idle durations as greater contributions to cost; penalty-based strategies aim for fair, stable, efficient scheduling</cite> <cite id="28b71dfc-2">Inserting idle time before jobs can decrease earliness and tardiness costs; finding the best schedule to minimize fines for being early or late is central to fair allocation</cite> <cite id="28b71dfc-3">Quality control disabled led to lateness 60× requested, underscoring sensitivity of scheduling systems to measurement and control</cite>. 
- Platform scheduling logic often privileges throughput and prediction error over worker well-being; absent constraints, algorithms can produce extreme lateness or unfair allocations, highlighting the need to encode temporal justice constraints into objectives and constraints <cite id="28b71dfc-3">Without quality control, lateness could be 60× requested lateness, illustrating instability and unfairness when measurement/control fail</cite>. 
- From a worker perspective, perceived algorithmic management comprises algorithmic monitoring intensity, stringency of reward/penalty rules, and order assignment volatility, all of which shape experienced urgency, pressure, and autonomy, and predictably affect mental health and turnover intentions <cite id="e793ee69-3">Perceived algorithmic management includes (1) monitoring intensity (location tracking, route recording, time monitoring), (2) reward/punishment stringency (ranking, fines, thresholds), and (3) order assignment volatility (fluctuations in quantity, convenience, time requirements); these shape pressure, urgency, uncertainty, and autonomy</cite> <cite id="e793ee69-3">Algorithmic systems are experienced as intensified labor control shaping workload pressure, temporal urgency, performance uncertainty, and perceived autonomy; perceived effects are shaped by how features are experienced, not only by formal parameters</cite>. 
- HCI design research shows that quantification elicits reactivity—workers change behavior in response to being measured—so systems that intensify measurement and narrow acceptable variance can self-reinforce control and bias outcomes, requiring calibrated thresholds, transparency, and contestability to avoid fairness failures <cite id="e793ee69-0">Reactivity to quantified metrics can become a new regime of control; workers’ responses (avoidance, adaptation, resistance) are shaped by quantification</cite>. 

Cross-disciplinary perspectives on justice and rights
- HR and organizational justice. Automating management removes human supervisors as arbiters, replacing them with opaque algorithms that disrupt procedural justice and perceived organizational support, calling for new governance models, transparency, and human-in-the-loop safeguards in algorithmic HR practices <cite id="f68a709a-3">Algorithmic management disrupts antecedents of supervisor support and procedural fairness; workers’ subjective interpretations of procedural justice are key; a new theory of perceived organizational support is required for algorithmically-managed gig work</cite> <cite id="f68a709a-2">Integrating labor process theory, the analysis shows algorithmic systems reenact power asymmetries while posing challenges to preserve worker dignity, transparency, and fairness</cite>. 
- Legal and policy perspectives. Systematic literature reviews highlight how algorithmic management impacts workers’ rights, justice, and welfare, underscoring the need for responsible, humane HR and policy responses, including limits on automated decision-making and protections for temporal rights like predictability and rest <cite id="f68a709a-4">A systematic review synthesizes how algorithms are used in managerial decision-making and their impacts on rights, justice, and welfare, encouraging responsible and humane HR policies</cite>. 
- Ethnographic and field-based evidence. In logistics and delivery, workers conceptualize algorithmic control as intensifying pressures on time, with perceived monitoring, volatility, and penalties predicting burnout and turnover; in warehouses, “algorithmic panopticon” dynamics compress labor into metrics while workers deploy tacit work games to negotiate control, revealing a dialectic of consent and resistance in temporal governance <cite id="e793ee69-3">Platform workers experience algorithmic systems as intensified labor control shaping urgency, uncertainty, and autonomy; these perceptions relate to psychological costs</cite> <cite id="e793ee69-4">Labor-tracking systems keep workers within an algorithmic panopticon, render labor as numbers, and workers’ tricks are forms of exerting agency and complying with managerial goals</cite>. 
- Organizational process view. Algorithmic management extends Taylorist principles—standardization, control, and efficiency—into continuous, multi-sensor surveillance and just-in-time optimization, while introducing new forms of social control (peer surveillance, traceability) that shift accountability and discipline time at scale <cite id="f68a709a-2">Algorithmic management shares efficiency, standardization, and control with Taylorism but adds software-mediated governance with asymmetric information</cite> <cite id="e793ee69-2">Digital systems in blue‑collar workplaces require documentation and shift accountability to workers; management employs peer-to-peer surveillance, formalized via TQM, to extend control</cite>. 

Implications and remedies for temporality justice
- Encode temporal rights into system design. Fair scheduling and penalty design must explicitly constrain temporal ownership violations (e.g., no forced real-time assignment during protected times, transparent overtime triggers), and allocate tasks with predictable windows, rest buffers, and fairness-aware objectives to avoid penalizing vulnerable workers for systemic uncertainty <cite id="ec3d7b1f-4">Algorithms appropriate temporal ownership through compulsory assignment and overtime penalties; design should restore substantive control over time boundaries</cite> <cite id="28b71dfc-1">Dynamic idle-time penalties can be tuned to balance exploration/exploitation and distribute costs fairly across idle and throughput objectives</cite>. 
- Provide transparency, explainability, and contestability. Workers need auditable reasons for scoring and penalties, access to baselines and calibration data, and mechanisms to appeal or adjust metrics, because opacity transforms systems from tools into opaque authorities that undermine procedural justice <cite id="ec3d7b1f-1">Algorithms create knowledge and power imbalances favoring the platform; collected performance data and tracking enable control</cite> <cite id="f68a709a-3">Opaque, complex processes disrupt procedural justice and perceived organizational support; new theory and safeguards are needed</cite>. 
- Calibrate “reactivity” and measurement thresholds. Because quantification elicits behavioral change, thresholds for monitoring and penalties should be set with social science input, with built-in safeguards to prevent self-fulfilling compliance cycles, punitive defaults, and stress-induced performance drops <cite id="e793ee69-0">Workers’ reactivity to quantification can become a new regime of control; design and regulation should anticipate and shape reactivity</cite>. 
- Human-in-the-loop governance and collective bargaining. Combine automated dispatching with human supervisors or unions to arbitrate time disputes, review fairness drift, and negotiate temporal norms (rest, predictability, shift patterns) as binding constraints, recognizing that algorithmic panopticons can be softened by co-present oversight and negotiated rules <cite id="e793ee69-4">In fulfillment centers, co-present managerial oversight alongside digital tracking shapes reactions; workers’ consented and collective tactics can mitigate control</cite> <cite id="e793ee69-2">Peer surveillance and traceability shift accountability; negotiated governance can rebalance accountability and control</cite>. 
- Regulate metrics and data governance. Platform rules, ranking systems, and idle-time/lateness penalties should be auditable for temporal fairness; data used to predict “optimal” schedules should include worker-context variables and constraints to avoid racialized or gendered temporal profiling, aligning with broader evidence that algorithmic systems reproduce historical inequities when fairness is not explicitly engineered <cite id="f68a709a-0">Algorithms perpetuate distributive and procedural injustices by reproducing historical inequalities or prioritizing efficiency over fairness; justice must be explicitly safeguarded</cite> <cite id="ec3d7b1f-3">Algorithmic matching and controlling mechanisms embed ranking, incentives, and penalties that condition workers’ temporal experiences</cite>. 

Limits, contingencies, and open questions
- Benefits and trade-offs. The specific functions of algorithmic management vary according to the work context, but algorithms typically include directing workers to their tasks and assigning them work schedules. Using algorithmic management can improve workplace fairness and efficiency by automating routine tasks and providing datadriven decision-making [9,84]. For this reason, many companies adopt algorithmic management in their workplaces to enhance worker productivity and oversee optimization on a large scale, ultimately increasing profits [18]. In addition, algorithmic management can reduce workers' workloads and create opportunities for worker self-improvement and career advancement [51]. Moreover, algorithms' predictable and systematic work direction and evaluation can decrease workers' stress [9].

In particular, algorithmic management can negatively impact work practices by giving employers and platforms more control and power [69]. Additionally, it could control worker behaviors through surveillance for task compliance, algorithmic opacity, behavioral nudges, and rigid evaluation measures [5,48]. 

Increased control and monitoring by algorithmic systems could reduce workers' discretion [36]. This persistent surveillance, which may carry significant consequences, such as layoffs, is often perceived as hostile by workers [65]. In addition, this surveillance can be further intensified by the opacity of the algorithmic systems [10,17,28]. Workers often struggle to comprehend the operational processes of algorithmic systems, leading to confusion about the reasons for following algorithmic directions or the potential consequences of non-compliance [49,64,67]. Specifically, LPT provides political economic grounding for studying invisible work. It also offers explanatory power that complements HCI's descriptive norms and interventionist orientation. Title: Algorithmic Management in the Logistics and Delivery Industry: An Empirical Study of Riders’ Job Burnout and Turnover Intention
Snippet: Algorithmic management refers to the use of data-driven digital systems to allocate tasks, monitor workers, evaluate performance, and administer rewards and penalties. In platform-based labor settings, algorithmic management often substitutes for direct human supervision by embedding control mechanisms into digital interfaces, delivery dispatching systems, ranking rules, and performance metrics [7,8]. This form of management has become especially prominent in the logistics and delivery industry, where platform companies rely on real-time tracking, dynamic scheduling, and automated performance control to coordinate large numbers of riders efficiently. 

Existing studies suggest that algorithmic management may enhance operational efficiency while also generating substantial psychological and behavioral costs for workers . In particular, platform workers may experience algorithmic systems not merely as neutral technical tools, but as forms of intensified labor control that shape workload pressure, temporal urgency, performance uncertainty, and perceived autonomy [9]. In this study, the term perceived refers to riders' subjective evaluations and interpretations of platform algorithmic control practices rather than objectively observed technical system parameters. This distinction is important because workers' psychological and behavioral reactions are shaped not only by formal system features, but also by how such features are experienced in everyday work. 

To capture this subjective experience more precisely, the present study conceptualizes perceived algorithmic management as comprising three related dimensions. The first is algorithmic monitoring intensity, referring to riders' perceptions of real-time digital surveillance such as location tracking, route recording, and working-time monitoring. The second is the stringency of reward and punishment rules, referring to workers' perceptions of the severity of ranking systems, fines, and incentive thresholds. The third is order assignment volatility, referring to perceived instability in task dispatching, including fluctuations in order quantity, route convenience, and delivery-time requirements. By distinguishing among these dimensions, the present study seeks to provide a more fine-grained understanding of how riders experience algorithmic control in their daily work.

Title: Fulfillment of the Work Games: Warehouse Workers' Experiences with Algorithmic Management
Snippet: While recent CSCW and HCI studies offer a rich understanding of workers' experiences under algorithmic management, these insights are predominantly based on the experiences of workers doing platform-mediated gig work. To broaden the empirical base for algorithmic critique, we conducted an ethnographic study of workers' experiences with algorithmic management and control within the context of an Amazon fulfillment center. In this context, workers are subject to algorithmic technologies of monitoring and control in the form of a assembled labor-tracking system and its corresponding metrics. 

We showed how the labor-tracking system integrates productivity metrics, a myriad of devices, and product and badge barcodes to keep workers within an algorithmic panopticon. Furthermore, we described how humans are required to resolve the discrepancies between the labor tracked by the system and the actual labor input. Our findings also demonstrate that the labor tracking systems in place in FCs tend to obscure human workers by rendering their labor as numbers. Finally, we detailed the various tricks employed by human workers to resist these labor tracking systems and the imposition of becoming enumerated. We contextualize these findings within the existing literature of CSCW and other relevant fields, elucidating how the distinct experiences and reactions of FC workers are influenced both by the characteristics of traditional work environment (i.e., co-present managerial oversight) and platform environments (i.e., nearly ubiquitous digital tracking). 

Through the lens of work games, we discussed how the various "tricks" that FC workers engage in are simultaneously forms of exerting creative agency and complying with managerial goals. We identified three patterns in workers' work games: active consenting-resistance, passive consentingresistance, and non-consenting resistance. Based on our analysis, we argue that investigating workers' concurrent resistance and consent helps us understand workers' experiences and reactions to algorithms with greater clarity and sympathy. Both are necessary if we are to design a better future for workers in any environment.

Below is a synthesis of the main findings on temporality justice under algorithmic management—how algorithmic systems configure work and time, how that produces temporal injustices, how workers experience and resist them, and what remedies and design principles are emerging across management, HCI, sociology, and legal/HR perspectives.

Defining temporality justice in algorithmic management
- Algorithmic management shifts core managerial functions—monitoring, scheduling, goal-setting, performance management, compensation, and termination—into automated systems that operate on real-time data and predictive analytics, often reducing or removing human discretion in the loop <cite id="f68a709a-2">In contrast, algorithmic management entrusts managerial functions such as monitoring, performance assessment, scheduling, goal‑setting, compensation, and even dismissal to algorithms and automated systems</cite> <cite id="f68a709a-2">Enabled by real‑time data collection, predictive analytics, and digital platforms, algorithmic management enables organizations to manage dispersed labor at scale with unprecedented precision</cite> <cite id="ec3d7b1f-3">AM refers to the use of increasingly intelligent algorithms to automate and optimize coordination and control; Parent‑Rocheleau and Parker identified six main functions: monitoring, goal setting, performance management, scheduling, compensation, and job termination</cite>. 
- Justice concerns arise because algorithmic neutrality is an illusion: optimization embodies normative assumptions about performance, risk, and merit, and can reproduce distributive and procedural injustices absent discriminatory intent <cite id="f68a709a-0">Empirical research demonstrates that algorithmic systems can perpetuate distributive and procedural injustices by reproducing historical inequalities or prioritizing efficiency over fairness; justice must be explicitly articulated and safeguarded within managerial decision frameworks</cite>. 
- Temporality justice focuses on whether algorithmic systems fairly govern rhythms, pacing, waiting, and the boundaries between work time and personal time; it asks whether control over time is distributed fairly and whether workers can plan, consent to, and contest temporal demands <cite id="ec3d7b1f-2">Algorithms act as machines that make time logically controllable and produce measurable time effects and rhythms; real‑time effects unfold as specific temporal conditions composed by different patterns of pace with socio‑technical arrangements</cite> <cite id="ec3d7b1f-4">Algorithmic time politics refers to asymmetric power relations established through systematic manipulation of temporal rhythm, allocation, and ownership, producing damaging effects across physiological, mental, and occupational safety dimensions</cite>.

Mechanisms that shape temporal control and justice
- Real-time quantification and surveillance. Platforms and systems track location, routes, working time, and every step, turning performance into streams of quantified data that are compared to baselines and projected into predictions to direct and evaluate work <cite id="ec3d7b1f-1">Digital systems meticulously organize, monitor, and measure work; performance data, working hours, and shifts are stored and visualized; tracking mechanisms are crucial for workforce management and create knowledge-asymmetry power imbalances favoring the platform</cite> <cite id="ec3d7b1f-3">Algorithms assign tasks, communicate with workers, and evaluate performance; algorithmic matching and controlling are core mechanisms</cite>. 
- Opacity and triangular visibility. Automated systems create information asymmetries—employers and often algorithm designers hold more knowledge than workers—undermining procedural justice and perceived organizational support that depends on accessible, fair processes <cite id="f68a709a-2">Algorithmic systems create triangular visibility regimes with information asymmetries where employers and algorithm designers hold more knowledge than workers</cite> <cite id="f68a709a-3">As algorithmic efficiencies minimize human intervention, workers’ interpretations of procedural justice are disrupted, implying a new theory of perceived organizational support for gig work</cite>. 
- Ranking, penalties, and volatility. Control is enforced through numeric rankings, fines, and dynamic dispatching that can shift workload intensity and timing unpredictably, shaping workers’ expectations and agency over time <cite id="ec3d7b1f-3">AM integrates algorithmic matching and controlling; ranking systems, fines, and incentives are used for performance governance</cite> <cite id="ec3d7b1f-4">Compulsory task-assignment and overtime penalty mechanisms appropriate workers’ temporal ownership; dynamic scheduling renders rhythms non‑standardized and instantaneous</cite>. 

Main findings on temporality justice

Temporal ownership: control over work-life boundaries and consent
- Algorithmic systems increasingly appropriate workers’ temporal ownership—the substantive capacity to decide how and when their time is used—even when legal contracts classify them as independent, by compulsory assignment, opaque ranking, and fragmented waiting, leaving workers with hollow autonomy over their schedules <cite id="ec3d7b1f-4">Algorithms de facto appropriate workers’ temporal ownership via compulsory task-assignment, overtime penalty mechanisms, and fragmented waiting; “ownership” here refers to substantive control over how time is used, which is hollowed out despite independent contractor status</cite>. 
- This erosion of temporal ownership is experienced as intensified control: workers face real-time tracking and automated penalties for deviations, reducing the predictability of when work begins and ends and compressing personal and work time <cite id="ec3d7b1f-1">Tracking mechanisms store and visualize performance data and shifts; algorithmic monitoring and real-time tracking create knowledge-asymmetry power imbalances</cite> <cite id="f68a709a-2">The shift from human oversight to software-mediated governance introduces asymmetries and reenacts power asymmetries with new challenges for worker autonomy and organizational justice</cite>. 
- Resistance emerges through work “games”—patterns of consented or non-consented tactics to negotiate the system’s rules—showing that while platforms automate control, workers simultaneously exercise agency to reclaim small temporal leeway within constrained spaces <cite id="e793ee69-4">In an Amazon fulfillment center, labor-tracking systems render labor as numbers and workers deploy active/passive consenting-resistance and non-consenting resistance; analyzing concurrent consent and resistance clarifies reactions to algorithms</cite> <cite id="e793ee69-0">HCI work emphasizes that workers’ reactivity to quantified metrics can become new regimes of control; understanding everyday impacts and counteractions is necessary to design regulatory interventions</cite>.

Temporal rhythm: speed, unpredictability, and psychosocial harm
- Dynamic scheduling and predictive control instantaneously shift task availability, producing non-standardized, unpredictable rhythms that undermine workers’ ability to allocate energy and plan, increasing alertness and stress and degrading psychosocial conditions <cite id="ec3d7b1f-4">Dynamic scheduling renders temporal rhythms non-standardized, instantaneous, and unpredictable; unpredictability prevents workers from planning energy allocation, maintaining a state of alertness and stress</cite>. 
- Empirical studies in platform delivery show algorithmic management increases demands and reduces control, with combined effects on mental and physical health; unpredictability of rhythm is a core driver of strain <cite id="ec3d7b1f-4">Mbare et al. found algorithmic management increases work demands, reduces work control, and restricts support, producing negative psychosocial effects; unpredictability of rhythm means workers cannot plan busy/idle periods or finish times</cite>. 
- Across industries, the integration of passive “stochastic machine witnesses” and active monitoring shifts accountability to workers, compressing rhythm into continuous measurable streams that normalize speed and punish latency <cite id="e793ee69-2">Contemporary monitoring is mediated by stochastic machine witnesses; systems require workers to document tasks and shift accountability onto them, extending control across channels</cite>. 
- HCI and STS theories emphasize that algorithms do not just measure time; they “make time” and generate new rhythms and cadences, shaping what counts as punctual, productive, and deviant, and producing temporal inequalities that are not self-evident to workers <cite id="ec3d7b1f-2">Algorithms inherit and impart orders as a continuous string of interpenetrating prior and subsequent actions; they are algorhythms that make time controllable and produce measurable time effects and rhythms; real-time does not mean a flat “now,” but specific patterns of pace</cite>.

Temporal allocation: fairness in scheduling, waiting, and penalties
- Fairness is entangled with optimization trade-offs: penalties for idleness or lateness, and weights for job completion times, can systematically disadvantage some workers depending on how costs are modeled, revealing the normative embedding of “fairness” in objective functions <cite id="28b71dfc-1">Dynamic idle time penalty mechanisms adapt penalty weights over iterations to balance exploration and exploitation, treating longer idle durations as greater contributions to cost; penalty-based strategies aim for fair, stable, efficient scheduling</cite> <cite id="28b71dfc-2">Inserting idle time before jobs can decrease earliness and tardiness costs; finding the best schedule to minimize fines for being early or late is central to fair allocation</cite> <cite id="28b71dfc-3">Quality control disabled led to lateness 60× requested, underscoring sensitivity of scheduling systems to measurement and control</cite>. 
- Platform scheduling logic often privileges throughput and prediction error over worker well-being; absent constraints, algorithms can produce extreme lateness or unfair allocations, highlighting the need to encode temporal justice constraints into objectives and constraints <cite id="28b71dfc-3">Without quality control, lateness could be 60× requested lateness, illustrating instability and unfairness when measurement/control fail</cite>. 
- From a worker perspective, perceived algorithmic management comprises algorithmic monitoring intensity, stringency of reward/penalty rules, and order assignment volatility, all of which shape experienced urgency, pressure, and autonomy, and predictably affect mental health and turnover intentions <cite id="e793ee69-3">Perceived algorithmic management includes (1) monitoring intensity (location tracking, route recording, time monitoring), (2) reward/punishment stringency (ranking, fines, thresholds), and (3) order assignment volatility (fluctuations in quantity, convenience, time requirements); these shape pressure, urgency, uncertainty, and autonomy</cite> <cite id="e793ee69-3">Algorithmic systems are experienced as intensified labor control shaping workload pressure, temporal urgency, performance uncertainty, and perceived autonomy; perceived effects are shaped by how features are experienced, not only by formal parameters</cite>. 
- HCI design research shows that quantification elicits reactivity—workers change behavior in response to being measured—so systems that intensify measurement and narrow acceptable variance can self-reinforce control and bias outcomes, requiring calibrated thresholds, transparency, and contestability to avoid fairness failures <cite id="e793ee69-0">Reactivity to quantified metrics can become a new regime of control; workers’ responses (avoidance, adaptation, resistance) are shaped by quantification</cite>. 

Cross-disciplinary perspectives on justice and rights
- HR and organizational justice. Automating management removes human supervisors as arbiters, replacing them with opaque algorithms that disrupt procedural justice and perceived organizational support, calling for new governance models, transparency, and human-in-the-loop safeguards in algorithmic HR practices <cite id="f68a709a-3">Algorithmic management disrupts antecedents of supervisor support and procedural fairness; workers’ subjective interpretations of procedural justice are key; a new theory of perceived organizational support is required for algorithmically-managed gig work</cite> <cite id="f68a709a-2">Integrating labor process theory, the analysis shows algorithmic systems reenact power asymmetries while posing challenges to preserve worker dignity, transparency, and fairness</cite>. 
- Legal and policy perspectives. Systematic literature reviews highlight how algorithmic management impacts workers’ rights, justice, and welfare, underscoring the need for responsible, humane HR and policy responses, including limits on automated decision-making and protections for temporal rights like predictability and rest <cite id="f68a709a-4">A systematic review synthesizes how algorithms are used in managerial decision-making and their impacts on rights, justice, and welfare, encouraging responsible and humane HR policies</cite>. 
- Ethnographic and field-based evidence. In logistics and delivery, workers conceptualize algorithmic control as intensifying pressures on time, with perceived monitoring, volatility, and penalties predicting burnout and turnover; in warehouses, “algorithmic panopticon” dynamics compress labor into metrics while workers deploy tacit work games to negotiate control, revealing a dialectic of consent and resistance in temporal governance <cite id="e793ee69-3">Platform workers experience algorithmic systems as intensified labor control shaping urgency, uncertainty, and autonomy; these perceptions relate to psychological costs</cite> <cite id="e793ee69-4">Labor-tracking systems keep workers within an algorithmic panopticon, render labor as numbers, and workers’ tricks are forms of exerting agency and complying with managerial goals</cite>. 
- Organizational process view. Algorithmic management extends Taylorist principles—standardization, control, and efficiency—into continuous, multi-sensor surveillance and just-in-time optimization, while introducing new forms of social control (peer surveillance, traceability) that shift accountability and discipline time at scale <cite id="f68a709a-2">Algorithmic management shares efficiency, standardization, and control with Taylorism but adds software-mediated governance with asymmetric information</cite> <cite id="e793ee69-2">Digital systems in blue‑collar workplaces require documentation and shift accountability to workers; management employs peer-to-peer surveillance, formalized via TQM, to extend control</cite>. 

Implications and remedies for temporality justice
- Encode temporal rights into system design. Fair scheduling and penalty design must explicitly constrain temporal ownership violations (e.g., no forced real-time assignment during protected times, transparent overtime triggers), and allocate tasks with predictable windows, rest buffers, and fairness-aware objectives to avoid penalizing vulnerable workers for systemic uncertainty <cite id="ec3d7b1f-4">Algorithms appropriate temporal ownership through compulsory assignment and overtime penalties; design should restore substantive control over time boundaries</cite> <cite id="28b71dfc-1">Dynamic idle-time penalties can be tuned to balance exploration/exploitation and distribute costs fairly across idle and throughput objectives</cite>. 
- Provide transparency, explainability, and contestability. Workers need auditable reasons for scoring and penalties, access to baselines and calibration data, and mechanisms to appeal or adjust metrics, because opacity transforms systems from tools into opaque authorities that undermine procedural justice <cite id="ec3d7b1f-1">Algorithms create knowledge and power imbalances favoring the platform; collected performance data and tracking enable control</cite> <cite id="f68a709a-3">Opaque, complex processes disrupt procedural justice and perceived organizational support; new theory and safeguards are needed</cite>. 
- Calibrate “reactivity” and measurement thresholds. Because quantification elicits behavioral change, thresholds for monitoring and penalties should be set with social science input, with built-in safeguards to prevent self-fulfilling compliance cycles, punitive defaults, and stress-induced performance drops <cite id="e793ee69-0">Workers’ reactivity to quantification can become a new regime of control; design and regulation should anticipate and shape reactivity</cite>. 
- Human-in-the-loop governance and collective bargaining. Combine automated dispatching with human supervisors or unions to arbitrate time disputes, review fairness drift, and negotiate temporal norms (rest, predictability, shift patterns) as binding constraints, recognizing that algorithmic panopticons can be softened by co-present oversight and negotiated rules <cite id="e793ee69-4">In fulfillment centers, co-present managerial oversight alongside digital tracking shapes reactions; workers’ consented and collective tactics can mitigate control</cite> <cite id="e793ee69-2">Peer surveillance and traceability shift accountability; negotiated governance can rebalance accountability and control</cite>. 
- Regulate metrics and data governance. Platform rules, ranking systems, and idle-time/lateness penalties should be auditable for temporal fairness; data used to predict “optimal” schedules should include worker-context variables and constraints to avoid racialized or gendered temporal profiling, aligning with broader evidence that algorithmic systems reproduce historical inequities when fairness is not explicitly engineered <cite id="f68a709a-0">Algorithms perpetuate distributive and procedural injustices by reproducing historical inequalities or prioritizing efficiency over fairness; justice must be explicitly safeguarded</cite> <cite id="ec3d7b1f-3">Algorithmic matching and controlling mechanisms embed ranking, incentives, and penalties that condition workers’ temporal experiences</cite>. 

Limits, contingencies, and open questions
- Benefits and trade-offs. Algorithms can increase transparency and reduce subjective bias in some contexts, and workers report reduced workloads or clearer criteria in certain settings; however, these gains often coexist with intensified surveillance, opacity, and asymmetric power that shape perceptions and lived conditions <cite id="e793ee69-1">Automation can improve fairness and efficiency and reduce workload and stress, but many studies find it shifts power to platforms and employers and introduces rigid evaluations and opacity that undermine autonomy</cite> <cite id="e793ee69-1">Algorithmic management can decrease workers’ stress via predictable, systematic direction and evaluation, yet it reshapes complex work practices and intensifies control</cite>. 
- Variability across jobs. Temporal governance under algorithms differs by industry and context—warehouses, call centers, and gig work exhibit distinct rhythms and metrics—so temporality justice requires context-specific audits and participatory design with worker representation to balance throughput with human temporal needs <cite id="f68a709a-2">The impacts of algorithmic management are complex and dual; consequences depend on sociotechnical design and implementation choices</cite> <cite id="ec3d7b1f-4">Platform labor’s algorithmic time politics produce asymmetric temporal control across rhythm, allocation, and ownership</cite>. 
- Research gaps. HCI and STS emphasize that we need more empirical studies that center worker interpretations and counteractions, and design frameworks that translate temporal rights (predictability, consent, rest, contestability) into measurable system constraints and governance processes <cite id="e793ee69-0">HCI calls for examining productivity monitoring technologies to understand impacts and design/regulatory interventions, foregrounding worker experiences and counteractions</cite>. 

In short, temporality justice under algorithmic management turns on whether systems fairly distribute control over time, pace, and allocation; current evidence shows that opaque, real-time quantification, ranking, and penalties systematically compress worker temporal autonomy, produce unpredictable rhythms and stress, and embed efficiency-driven objectives that can bias fairness without explicit safeguards. Effective remedies combine transparent, contestable metrics; fairness-aware scheduling and penalty design; human-in-the-loop governance; and negotiated temporal norms, implemented with worker participation and audited for temporal inequalities across contexts <cite id="ec3d7b1f-1">Algorithmic infrastructures collect and visualize performance, working hours, and shifts, enabling control and creating knowledge-asymmetry power imbalances</cite> <cite id="ec3d7b1f-4">Systematic manipulation of temporal rhythm, allocation, and ownership yields predictable harms; restoring temporal ownership and rhythm requires governance that reconfigures algorithmic control</cite> <cite id="f68a709a-0">Algorithmic neutrality is illusory; justice must be explicitly articulated and safeguarded in managerial frameworks</cite> <cite id="e793ee69-3">Perceived monitoring, volatility, and penalties shape urgency and autonomy, predicting burnout and turnover</cite> <cite id="e793ee69-4">Workers’ consented and collective tactics reveal agency within algorithmic panopticons, suggesting pathways for fairer temporal governance</cite>.</answer>
